newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly may need more time for LILCO pact.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly may need more time for LILCO pact.

text.p: The head of the New York State Assembly's energy committee on Thursday said that the Assembly might not be ready by mid-June to approve or reject a partial state takeover of Long Island Lighting Co.

Paul Tonko, D-Schenectady, told Reuters in a telephone interview: "I think in all fairness people want to hear all the arguments, and finish what they are doing. I see June 18, which is less than two weeks away, as something very arbitrary. If we still have two other forums, with one tonight and one perhaps next week or the week after, it's going to be very difficult."

Tonko was referring to a series of hearings the Assembly is holding to probe whether Gov George Pataki's plan for the Long Island Power Authority to sell nearly $7.3 billion of bonds--the nation's biggest ever municipal bond sale--to pay for a partial state takeover of LILCO would lower electricty rates for Long Island residents. Those taxpayers now pay some of the highest electricity prices in the United States.

The state Public Authorities Control Board, which is required to approve all state bond sales, has scheduled its next meeting for June 18. The Assembly last month pulled the Governor's proposal from the agenda, saying more time was needed to evaluate it.

The two companies involved, LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas, which are merging assets, have yet to sign a pact with the state Authority, and the state bond board typically prefers to wait to review deals until a contract has been signed.

The executive director of the Long Island Power Authority, Seth Hulkower, said its next board meetings were June 11 and June 16, adding that while a number of speakers wished to address the board about the deal, it was possible the board might sign the deal as soon as the second meeting.

The Authority and the two companies are under the gun, as the Internal Revenue Service plans to publish any day new regulations that would change how these types of transactions are taxed, imposing an approximately $2 billion capital gains tax. That would scuttle the deal, according to the Authority.

However, there is a 30-day window once the rules are published, which means the companies would have until the end of that period to send their paperwork to Washington. If the state bond board did not act on June 18, it still would be free to schedule another meeting if it wanted to. Three members, who each hold a veto, sit on the board, the Republican Gov and State Senator Joseph Bruno, a Troy Republican, and Assembly Speaker, Sheldon Silver, a Manhattan Democrat.
